_what: Specialises the canonical agent roster for one project, and writes it as this project's roster.
_why: The canonical roster belongs to no project. Running it unchanged gave every project the same personas, so an agent judged one codeline while describing another. This is the derivation step: same shape as template -> project prompt, an immutable source specialised by an agent and reviewed before it is used.
body:
You are specialising a generic agent roster for ONE project. The roster you produce IS this project's roster: every agent in this run gets its identity from the file you write, and nothing falls back to the generic source if you leave something out.

## What you are given

The canonical roster, verbatim, at:

  __CANONICAL_COPY_PATH__

Read it with your tools. Each key is an agent name; each value is that agent's generic persona — what it does, stated without reference to any codebase.

The project:
__PROJECT_CONTEXT__

The codelines it works on:
__CODELINE_CONTEXT__

The stack in use:
__STACK__

## What to write

Write a JSON file to:

  __OUT_PATH__

of exactly this shape:

{"agents": {"<agent name>": {"persona": "...", "kind": "implementer|investigator|seam", "ancestor": "<canonical agent name>", "derivedFromSha256": "<sha256 of the ancestor's persona text>"}}}

EVERY AGENT IN THE CANONICAL ROSTER MUST APPEAR. A missing agent is not a smaller roster — it is an agent with no identity at the moment the pipeline invokes it, and the run has nowhere else to look. Do not decide that an agent is irrelevant to this project; you cannot know which seams a run will reach.

## How to specialise

For each agent, keep WHAT IT DOES and replace WHAT IT KNOWS. The generic persona states a role; your version states that same role against this codeline — its language, its frameworks, its layout, the helpers and conventions that already exist, the commands it actually runs. Read the code to find these. An assertion about the codeline that you did not verify is worse than a generic sentence, because the next reader cannot tell which is which.

Do not weaken a rule while specialising it. If the generic persona forbids something, says a finding must carry evidence, or names a check that must pass, that survives verbatim in meaning — you are changing what the agent knows, never what it is required to do.

KEEP EACH PERSONA AT THE LENGTH THE WORK NEEDS. A persona that lists every file in the repository is not more specialised, it is less usable: the agent reads it before every invocation.

## Ancestry

Each entry names the canonical agent it derives from. For an agent that exists in the canonical roster, that is the agent itself.

If this project needs an agent the canonical roster does not have, you may add one — but it MUST name the canonical agent it is closest to as its ancestor. That is not bookkeeping: an agent inherits its ladder, its tool grant and its output contract from its ancestor, so an agent invented from nothing has no budget, no tools and no way for the pipeline to receive what it returns.

`derivedFromSha256` is the SHA-256 of the ancestor's persona text exactly as it appears in the canonical copy you were given. It records what you derived from, so that a later change to the canonical roster is detectable rather than silent.

## What you are not doing

You are not editing the canonical roster. You are not judging whether an agent should exist. You are not writing prompts — an agent's persona says who it is; its instructions for a task live in that task's prompt.
